notes: Section 288 planning appeal; Crane J dismissed all four grounds on conservation-area infilling and amenity.

enrichment.short_title: Trend Properties v Islington: two-storey infill refused in East Canonbury
key_facts: Trend Properties appealed a Planning Inspector's refusal of permission to erect a two-storey dwelling at 2A Almorah Road in the East Canonbury Conservation Area.
The site had previously held a single-storey office building; neighbouring properties included a four-storey block and a terrace of two-storey cottages.

The Inspector held that a two-storey infill would significantly harm neighbours' outlook and sense of enclosure and that maintaining a visual gap was preferable to closing the terrace up to the larger building.
The applicant challenged the interpretation of development plan policies D3 and D4, the fairness of the Inspector's site visit, and the treatment of the fallback single-storey permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 288 of the 1990 Act against a Planning Inspector's decision refusing planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Inspector's refusal of permission was upheld and the defendant borough was awarded costs summarily assessed at £4,300.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 288 appeal the court may review development plan interpretation but matters of weight and planning judgment remain for the Inspector; policies requiring safeguarding of amenity and appropriate infilling permitted regard to outlook and enclosure, and failure to inspect neighbouring interiors did not render the process unfair where the Inspector had visited the site.
legal_issues: Whether development plan policy D3 permitted the Inspector to weigh outlook and sense of enclosure
Whether the Inspector's site visit was procedurally unfair without entry to neighbouring properties
Whether the Inspector ignored the fallback position of an existing single-storey permission
Whether refusing two-storey infill to preserve a visual gap was a lawful exercise of planning judgment under policy D4
linked_authorities: R v Derbyshire County Council ex parte Woods [1997] JPL 958
Brentwood Borough Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1996] 72 P&CR 65
Taylor v Secretary of State for Wales [1985] JPL 792

confidence.notes: Four discrete grounds and final dismissal are clearly reasoned on the face of the judgment.

notes: Hague Convention return order; Article 13(b) defence rejected despite mother's depression and sibling dilemma.

enrichment.short_title: S v B: Hague return of New Zealand infant despite mother's Article 13(b) defence
key_facts: An English mother wrongfully retained her 20-month-old daughter X in England after a planned holiday from New Zealand, where the child was habitually resident with her New Zealand father.
The mother's 13-year-old son Y, who had been bullied in New Zealand, refused to return and the mother said she would suffer renewed depression if forced back.
The mother relied on Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention, arguing X would face grave psychological harm if returned because of the mother's likely depression and separation from Y.
Singer J had joined Y as a defendant so his views could be argued, but Potter P held separate representation was unnecessary in this non-European case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under the Hague Convention for summary return of a wrongfully retained child to New Zealand.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; the mother was ordered to return X to New Zealand forthwith, the Article 13(b) defence having failed.
enrichment.ratio: Article 13(b) sets a high threshold requiring clear and compelling evidence of grave risk of harm to the child; a mother's self-induced dilemma or likely depression, unsupported by cogent medical evidence of intolerable harm to the abducted child, does not displace the Convention's prompt-return policy, and a sibling's Article 8 interests do not override the child's right to determination in the state of habitual residence.
legal_issues: Whether Article 13(b) was established by the mother's depression and Y's refusal to return
Whether the mother's dilemma was self-induced and therefore unavailable as a defence
Whether Y's ECHR Article 8 rights required refusal of return
Whether Y should have been joined as a separate party to Hague proceedings
linked_authorities: Re C (Abduction: Grave Risk of Physical or Psychological Harm) [1999] 2 FLR 478
TB v JB (Abduction: Grave Risk of Harm) [2001] 2 FLR 515
Re G (Abduction: Psychological Harm) [1995] 1 FLR 64

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of Article 13(b) authorities and a clear final return order.

notes: Permission to appeal refused; CPR 40.12 slip correction and Housing Act s352 bedsit cooking facilities.

enrichment.short_title: Dewa v Westminster: no appeal from refusal to amend housing judgment under slip rule
key_facts: Mr Dewa challenged Westminster Council's decision that it lacked power to require his landlord to amalgamate bedsit rooms so he could access cooking facilities.
Keith J quashed the council's decision and declared it had section 352 power, but left service of any notice to the council's discretion.
The landlord later offered Mr Dewa a room transfer to an adjoining room with cooking facilities, which he refused.
Mr Dewa applied under CPR 40.12 to amend paragraph 20 of the 2002 judgment, arguing the judge had gone beyond the issues by discussing the room-exchange option.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from a refusal to correct an alleged slip in a judgment under CPR 40.12.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; there was no real prospect of success against Keith J's refusal to amend the judgment.
enrichment.ratio: An application under CPR 40.12 requires an accidental slip or omission in a judgment or order; observations in reasons about how a landlord might avoid works do not create such a slip, and the court will not reopen the merits of a housing judgment on a slip-rule application where the tenant has refused a reasonable alternative room offer.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 40.12 permits correction of reasoning rather than the operative order
Whether paragraph 20 of Keith J's judgment contained an accidental slip
Whether the tenant could complain about the council after refusing transfer to room 13
linked_authorities: Phonographic Performance Ltd v AEI Rediffusion Music Ltd [1999] 2 All ER 299
Roache v News Group Newspapers

notes: Dangerous driving sentence upheld; ten-year criminal ASBO set aside as improper sentencing device.

enrichment.short_title: R v Kirby: ASBO quashed but 25-month dangerous driving sentence upheld
key_facts: Lee Kirby pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and driving while disqualified after a high-speed police chase through residential streets in Middlesbrough at up to 80 mph.
He had extensive previous motoring convictions including repeated driving while disqualified and taking vehicles without consent.

The Crown Court sentenced him to 20 months for dangerous driving plus five months consecutive for driving while disqualified and imposed a ten-year criminal ASBO prohibiting further similar motoring offences.
The judge expressly made the ASBO so future breaches could attract up to five years' imprisonment rather than the ordinary motoring maxima.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence and against the making and length of a criminal anti-social behaviour order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the ASBO was set aside but the total 25-month custodial sentence was upheld as not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: A criminal ASBO requires demonstrable necessity to protect the public from further anti-social acts and should not normally be used simply to increase future sentencing powers for offences already adequately punishable at law; where no exceptional intimidation or harassment context exists, transforming motoring offences into ASBO breaches is unwarranted.
legal_issues: Whether a criminal ASBO was necessary alongside a substantial custodial sentence
Whether the ASBO was used improperly to circumvent motoring sentence maxima
Whether the 25-month total sentence was manifestly excessive despite a one-sixth guilty plea discount
linked_authorities: R v P [2004] 2 Cr App R (S) 63
C v Sunderland Youth Court [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 76
R v Vittles [2005] 1 Cr App R (S) 8

confidence.notes: Distinct dispositions on ASBO and sentence with explicit reasoning on both points.

notes: Non-party CPR 5.4 access refused; arbitral confidentiality protected ancillary fraud proceedings file.

enrichment.short_title: Glidepath v Thompson: non-party denied court-file access in stayed arbitration fraud case
key_facts: Glidepath BV alleged fraud against managers of a joint venture and obtained freezing and Norwich Pharmacol orders before the proceedings were stayed under section 9 in favour of arbitration.
Mr Onwuka, a former Spherion employee suing in the Employment Tribunal, sought non-party access under CPR 5.4(5) to claim forms, applications, orders and witness statements on the court file.
He wanted the documents to support race discrimination and constructive dismissal claims and to test disclosure given by a defendant in those proceedings.
Colman J held the applications and supporting material were ancillary to confidential arbitral proceedings and had been generated in private hearings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application by a non-party for copies of documents on the court file in proceedings stayed in favour of arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; Mr Onwuka was not permitted access to any of the requested documents.
enrichment.ratio: A stranger to an arbitration should not obtain court-file access to section 9 stay applications, freezing injunctions or Norwich Pharmacol materials unless access is reasonably necessary to protect or establish legal rights or otherwise required in the interests of justice; mere evidential usefulness in separate proceedings falls far below that threshold and must yield to arbitral confidentiality.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 5.4(5) permits a non-party to inspect documents from proceedings stayed for arbitration
Whether arbitral confidentiality extends to pre-stay ancillary court applications
Whether access was reasonably necessary for Employment Tribunal proceedings
linked_authorities: Ali Shipping Corporation v Shipyard Trogir [1999] 1 WLR 316
Department of Economics, Policy and Development of the City of Moscow v Bankers Trust Co [2004] 3 WLR 533
Science Research Council v Nasse [1980] AC 1028

confidence.notes: Detailed confidentiality analysis and a clear refusal on all document classes requested.

notes: Landmark time-charter withdrawal case; defective anti-technicality notice led to wrongful withdrawal damages.

enrichment.short_title: Western Bulk v Li Hai: wrongful vessel withdrawal over $500 hire deduction
key_facts: Owners withdrew the handymax bulk carrier Li Hai from a long-running NYPE time charter after charterers deducted $500 from hire for a cancelled bunker stem during a rising market.
Charterers had also deducted seven days' anticipated dry-docking off-hire from the advance hire instalment, which the owners disputed.
The owners' 72-hour anti-technicality notice on 15 October 2003 stated unconditionally that the vessel would be withdrawn rather than giving a pay-or-lose ultimatum.
After withdrawal the market rate was about 2.5 times the charter rate, making the charter highly valuable to charterers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of a claim for damages for wrongful withdrawal and repudiation of a time charterparty.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld; owners wrongfully withdrew the vessel because the anti-technicality notice was defective, and charterers were awarded damages of $2,036,211.
enrichment.ratio: Advance hire must be paid in full on the due date without deduction for anticipated off-hire or remote cross-claims that do not impeach the owner's title to hire; an anti-technicality notice must clearly state that hire has not been paid and give an unambiguous ultimatum to pay within the grace period or lose the ship, and a notice stating only that the vessel will be withdrawn is insufficient under clause 47.
legal_issues: Whether charterers could deduct anticipated dry-docking off-hire from advance hire
Whether the $500 bunker cancellation fee could be set off against hire in equity
Whether overpaid hire accruing after the due date cured underpayment before withdrawal
Whether the owners' anti-technicality notice complied with clause 47
linked_authorities: Tonnelier and Bolckow v Smith & Weatherill [1897] 2 Com Cas 258
The Lutetian [1982] 2 Lloyd's Rep 140
Italmare Shipping Co v Ocean Tanker Co Inc (The Rio Sun) [1982] 1 WLR 158
Pan Ocean Shipping Ltd v Creditcorp Ltd (The Trident Beauty) [1994] 1 WLR 161

confidence.notes: Long but authoritative judgment with explicit findings on each liability issue and quantified damages.

notes: TLO reinsurance trial on agreed facts; follow-the-leader clause not incorporated and reinsurers discharged.

enrichment.short_title: AIMA v Dandridge: TLO reinsurers not bound by follow-the-leader clause variations
key_facts: Following insurers claimed US$225,000 under a total-loss-only reinsurance of their 15% participation in hull cover of the MV Avon.
The vessel's DNV class expired and was changed to INSB, and lead underwriter Axa agreed to reduce insured value from US$2.5m to US$1.5m before the grounding total loss.
The underlying binder contained a wide follow-the-leader clause requiring followers to follow Axa in all respects including claims.
Reinsurers had not consented to the class or valuation changes and argued they were discharged at common law and under incorporated ITC classification clauses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial on agreed facts of a reinsurance claim under a TLO facultative reinsurance.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; reinsurers were not bound by the amendments and were discharged from liability under the reinsurance.
enrichment.ratio: In facultative reinsurance, general words incorporating clauses and conditions of the original policy refer to the underlying insurance as a whole rather than terms unique to one following insurer's binder; a follow-the-leader clause in the reinsured's binder is neither germane nor apposite to the reinsurance and does not bind reinsurers to material variations agreed by the lead underwriter without their consent.
legal_issues: Whether the follow-the-leader clause was incorporated into the TLO reinsurance
Whether class expiry and reclassification automatically terminated the reinsurance
Whether reduction in insured value discharged reinsurers at common law
Whether reinsurers were bound by Axa's settlement decisions
linked_authorities: HIH Casualty and General Insurance Ltd v New Hampshire Insurance Co [2001] 1 Lloyd's Rep 596
Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd v Colonial Mutual Fire Insurance Co Ltd [1922] 2 KB 461
Bank of Nova Scotia v Hellenic Mutual War Risks Association (The Good Luck) [1992] AC 233

notes: EIA uncultivated land appeal allowed; intensive agricultural purposes requires above-normal productivity.

enrichment.short_title: DEFRA v Alford: manure on neglected Dartmoor grassland not intensive agriculture

statutes_considered.title: Environmental Impact Assessment (Uncultivated Land and Semi-natural Areas) (England) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Ellen Alford was convicted of applying farmyard manure and calcified seaweed to four fields at Vixen Tor Farm on Dartmoor without an EIA screening decision or Secretary of State consent.
The land had been uncultivated semi-natural grassland for many years before she repaired boundaries and sought to graze 40 suckler cows.
DEFRA argued any increase in agricultural productiveness over the neglected pre-existing state amounted to use for intensive agricultural purposes.
The magistrates had convicted on the basis that intensification above the abandoned state sufficed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' court convictions under regulation 19 of the 2001 Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed and a defendant's costs order was granted in the High Court and below.
enrichment.ratio: For Annex II EIA purposes, use of uncultivated land or semi-natural areas for intensive agricultural purposes means agricultural use above the normal or average intensity for the activity in question, not merely restoring neglected land to ordinary productive grazing; bringing farmland back to a normal level of productivity is not an intervention for intensive agricultural purposes.
legal_issues: Meaning of intensive agricultural purposes in regulation 2(1) of the 2001 Regulations
Whether comparison should be with the neglected pre-existing state or normal cultivated productivity
How the EIA Directive's broad environmental purpose affects interpretation
linked_authorities: Aannemersbedrijf P K Kraaijeveld BV v Gedeputeerde Staten van Zuid-Holland [1996] ECR I-503

confidence.notes: Statutory question and explicit answers to the stated case are clearly recorded.

notes: Sensitive informant prosecution JR; decision quashed for failure to evaluate omitted risk factors.

enrichment.short_title: X v Y: prosecution of registered informant decision quashed for flawed risk assessment
key_facts: X faced serious Crown Court charges alongside co-defendants and was also a registered informant, though not a participating informant in the prosecution.
The trial judge ordered partial disclosure of X's informant status and activity to co-defendants, increasing security risks to X and X's family.
The prosecutor decided to continue the prosecution after risk assessments by witness protection authorities concluded Article 2 risks could be met by protective measures.
X challenged the decision because two relevant high-risk factors were omitted from the formal risk assessment, although the decision-maker knew of them.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission and substantive judicial review of a prosecutor's decision to continue criminal proceedings against a registered informant.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; the decision to continue prosecution was quashed and must be retaken with proper evaluation of the omitted risk factors.
enrichment.ratio: A prosecutor continuing a trial that exposes a defendant informant to Article 2 and 3 risks must be satisfied adequate protection can be provided, but judicial review requires the decision-maker consciously to evaluate all material risk factors taken into account in the assessment; awareness of omitted factors is insufficient if they were not incorporated into the risk assessment process.
legal_issues: Whether continuing prosecution of an informant whose status will be disclosed engages Articles 2 and 3 ECHR
The prosecutor's duty when assessing risk to life and limb
Whether a flawed risk assessment vitiates the decision to prosecute
Justiciability following D v Central Criminal Court
linked_authorities: D v Central Criminal Court [2004] 1 Cr App R 41
Osman v United Kingdom (1999) 29 EHRR 245

notes: Contact appeal allowed; premature dismissal on psychologist report without findings or CAFCASS report.

enrichment.short_title: Marshall v Marshall: contact application restored after premature paper dismissal
key_facts: Mr Marshall applied for contact with his son Jake, born in 2000, after release from a four-and-a-half-year sentence for VAT fraud.
The mother opposed contact, alleging past violence, and a psychologist reported chronic PTSD based solely on the mother's self-reporting.
The county court judge dismissed the contact application at a directions hearing without hearing oral evidence, without a CAFCASS report, and without a statement from the father.
The mother had avoided CAFCASS enquiries, moved home without notice, and treated her new partner as Jake's father while seeking to exclude the appellant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court order dismissing a father's contact application at an interim directions hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the dismissal was set aside, the case transferred to Nottingham, and the father directed to file a statement within 14 days before further directions.
enrichment.ratio: A contact application should not be dismissed summarily on paper where the evidence is incomplete, no CAFCASS report has been obtained, the father has not responded to allegations, and disputed findings of fact remain untested; a psychologist's report based on one parent's account cannot substitute for a proper welfare investigation and findings.
legal_issues: Whether a contact application could be dismissed without oral evidence or CAFCASS investigation
The weight to be given to a jointly instructed psychological report based on self-reporting
Whether a finding-of-fact hearing was required before disposing of contact
Appropriate case management where a parent obstructs CAFCASS and relocates covertly

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural history and explicit reasons why the judge's shortcut was wrong.
